section_summary: The section concludes a report on the Yomiuri Newspaper with labor-contract provisions, Management Council bylaws, and a bibliography, then contains a major SCAP study of rural and urban circulation for 113 Japanese daily newspapers. The circulation study compares readership density across Japan’s prefectures and regions and supplies detailed tables, charts, rankings, distribution areas, and an index. The remaining correspondence concerns the proposed sale of a long run of the Mainichi Shimbun to an American research library and personnel changes intended to improve Pacific Stars and Stripes.

subfiles.title: The Yomiuri Newspaper: Appendix B and Sources
subfiles.from: Civil Information and Education Section, General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: This concluding portion documents the Yomiuri labor agreement, the joint Management Council, and the sources used for a study of the newspaper.
subfiles.summary: Yomiuri Appendix B: union members may take part in politics if it doesn't interfere with duties or editorial policy; a twelve-member Management Council, half management and half union, handles working conditions, personnel, pay, regulations and policy; the bibliography lists SCAP studies, records and interviews.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 301: Rural-Urban Circulation of Principal Dailies in Japan
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch forwards two copies of a SCAP special report on rural and urban newspaper circulation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 301 encloses two copies of Special Report AR-310-IM-102-PP-B-28 (May 5, 1948) from Civil Information and Education on rural-urban circulation of principal dailies; no more copies were available.

subfiles.title: Rural-Urban Circulation of Principal Dailies in Japan
subfiles.from: Information Media Branch, Research Unit, Analysis and Research Division, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: The report analyzes the rural and urban circulation of 113 principal Japanese daily newspapers as of September 1, 1947.
subfiles.summary: Using publisher returns supplied through the Japan Press Association and 1947 census figures, the study compares newspaper circulation per thousand inhabitants in rural and urban portions of every prefecture. It finds that rural newspaper supply was generally less than half the urban supply, with Kansai having the greatest circulation density and southern Japan the sparsest distribution. Extensive tables give circulation by newspaper and prefecture, while charts and appendices rank all 113 papers and identify their distribution areas.

subfiles.title: Personal Letter Concerning a Complete File of the Mainichi Shimbun
subfiles.about: Sebald asks whether an American library or university might purchase a nearly complete run of the Mainichi Shimbun from 1917 onward.
subfiles.summary: Sebald says a Japanese acquaintance offers a nearly complete Japanese-language Mainichi Shimbun file from June 17, 1917, in excellent condition except singed edges and about fifteen missing dates, asking about 400,000-500,000 yen, and suggests the Library of Congress or a university.

subfiles.title: Memorandum: Attached Letter
subfiles.about: Walton reports Harvard University Library’s preliminary interest in the Mainichi Shimbun collection offered through Sebald.
subfiles.summary: Walton discussed the offer with Harvard Library director Keyes Metcalf and expert Andrew Osborn, who found the price reasonable and said Harvard wants original Japanese sources; Harvard needs a week or ten days to consult John Fairbank.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 794: New Head for Pacific Stars and Stripes
subfiles.from: William J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch reports Major Fred W. May’s appointment to lead Pacific Stars and Stripes and explains the editorial and administrative problems prompting the change.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 794: journalists rate Pacific Stars and Stripes the weakest of Japan's four English papers; Major Fred May, a Missouri newspaperman, took charge December 13, 1948 to supervise editorial practices, leaving daily editing to M. H. Hathaway and George Hu, and to improve relations with public-relations officials.

subfiles.title: Letter Declining Purchase of the Mainichi Shimbun File
subfiles.from: Luther H. Evans, Librarian of Congress
subfiles.about: The Librarian of Congress declines for the present to buy the offered Mainichi Shimbun file because a microfilm copy may be obtainable.
subfiles.summary: Evans acknowledges the complete Mainichi Shimbun file in Tokyo from June 17, 1917, but, as Japanese newsprint is perishable and microfilm may be available, the Library won't buy the originals now; it may reconsider if no complete microfilm exists.

subfiles.title: Harvard College Library Letter on the Mainichi Shimbun
subfiles.about: Osborn reports that Harvard will not buy the offered Mainichi Shimbun collection and suggests approaching Yale or the Hoover Library.
subfiles.summary: Osborn couldn't persuade Harvard's Chinese-studies staff to buy the Mainichi Shimbun file; they hoped another library would, suggesting Yale then Hoover, and Harvard already holds the Asahi Shimbun that Dr. Chiu preferred.
